newsitem.title: USA: Dole predicts campaign finance reform next year.
newsitem.headline: Dole predicts campaign finance reform next year.

text.p: Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole said allegations of improper political fundraising hounding the Clinton campaign would prod Congress to finally reform U.S. campaign finance laws next year.

In an interview taped on Friday and due to be released on Sunday, Dole denied that he opposed campaign finance reform, as President Bill Clinton charged on Friday, but said previous attempts to fix the system were hampered by his colleagues.

Clinton, battered by allegations that his Democratic Party improperly accepted large contributions from foreign interests, on Friday proposed major reform of campaign finance laws including banning contributions by non-citizens.

"Now, with the foreign money coming in, I think it will spur campaign reform just like we had campaign reform after Watergate," Dole told ABC-TV's "This Week with David Brinkley" program in an interview taped on Friday to air on Sunday.
Excerpts of the interview were released late on Saturday.
"We didn't go far enough, apparently. But now this is another opportunity and this will be a stimulus," said Dole. "I think it will bring about campaign reform next year."

Dole said a "bipartisan, non-partisan" commission was needed to recommend reforms since "when Republicans are in charge, we want to make it better for us, and (when) Democrats (are) in charge, they want to make it better to them."
Clinton called for voluntary spending limits for congressional races and endorsed a ban on contributions to political parties from foreign corporations and individuals.

Dole called for a ban on contributions by non-citizens, a ban on contributions to political parties by corporations and labor unions, and said steps should be considered to limit the influence of political action committees.
He also called for measures to limit trade unions' ability to contribute membership dues to political campaigns.
In order to get the reforms through, Dole said the leaders of Congress would have to ban amendments on the legislation.
"Congress has to vote up or down, no amendments, otherwise ... we may never have reform or much of it will never happen," Dole said.
He acknowledged that Republicans had been faulted for their opposition to campaign finance reform, but said the issue would be a priority if he was elected on Nov. 5.

"I know members of my party resist this, they don't like campaign finance reform. They like the present system," Dole said, "But I think there are changes we can make that will help ensure that the election belongs to the people."

Democrats have also raised questions about fund-raising by the Republican Party, citing large contributions to the Republicans by British tobacco and oil companies, as well as a guilty plea by a senior Dole campaign official to charges involving improper handling of campaign contributions.
